title: Harvard, Anthropic, and QuEra Breakthrough Research Uniquely Shows AI Can Reduce the Resources Quantum Applications Need, Significantly Accelerating the Era of Useful Quantum Computing
body:
The research preprint, "Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models" (arXiv:2610.22367), examines eight computational building blocks used in larger quantum algorithms. In seven, AI-designed circuits reduced both gate counts and qubit requirements relative to the corresponding baseline designs. In the eighth, the search found a new approach that offers additional choices between qubit requirements and gate counts. The research, reflecting an industry-first [...] Numerical computation: A fixed-point Gaussian function was also substantially changed. AI achieved a 39x reduction in the combined resource metric, the largest in the paper, with Toffoli gates down from about 24,000 to 1,583 and qubits from 362 to 139. [...] Useful quantum computing arrives where two curves meet. One is hardware capability, which rises as machines gain more qubits and more reliable operations. The other is the resources useful algorithms require, which fall as those algorithms are made more efficient. Progress on either curve moves the meeting point earlier; progress on both can bring valuable applications within reach sooner. This research addresses the second curve.

body: Spyre is IBM’s dataflow AI accelerator, optimized for inference. It is designed for enterprise teams running AI alongside their applications and data on IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power systems. Its reduced-precision compute is well suited to the matrix-heavy work in language generation and embedding models. Unlike a conventional GPU, which executes kernels as instruction streams across scheduled groups of threads, Spyre triggers computation as data arrives at its compute engines. PyTorch provides [...] AI is increasingly being embedded in the systems that process transactions, detect fraud, analyze claims, and assist employees. And with this growing usage, the AI hardware ecosystem is expanding. GPUs remain central to modern AI, but they are increasingly joined by accelerators with different architectures, execution models, and performance characteristics. Giving developers more choices requires more than building new chips. The software ecosystem must make new accelerators usable without [...] Spyre is an out-of-tree accelerator, rather than one of the GPU platforms most commonly supported by AI software. Spyre relies on TorchDynamo to trace a model graph and TorchInductor to lower that graph into representations optimized for the target hardware. Within vLLM, extension mechanisms such as CustomOp and PluggableLayer allow a hardware plugin to customize behavior without reimplementing large portions of the software stack.

title: 22 U.S.C. § 10301: United States international cyberspace policy
A New Agenda for Tech Regulation Beyond AI | TechPolicy.Press
body:
Caplan says, “We’re not going to stop the dead internet, but we should at least know how much of the internet is dead.” More pragmatically, while the FTC prohibits fake social media influence, it doesn’t require disclosure. Thus, advertisers, many of whom are small businesses, are getting charged for bot clicks even when they’re told they’re not. [...] Data centers are the Achilles heel of the tech industry: they’re a visible place where people can focus their efforts to curb the power of big social media platforms and AI companies. But regulating data centers, or even AI, is by no means the only form of technology regulation that we need. Given this overwhelming voter mandate to enact tech regulation, I asked some of the top scholars and policy folks in this space one question: what’s on your wishlist to regulate technology, at either the [...] – – –

As civil society organizations, thinktanks, and policy shops scramble to readjust their policy priorities in the wake of this week’s election, it is important to think beyond AI. Expanding regulatory capacity, passing comprehensive privacy legislation, and mandating data access for researchers may not be flashy, but these policies will have real-world implications for technology companies and, potentially, enormous benefits for the average American.
